title: NPV: Net Present Value
subtitle: Does the project create value? NPV gives the answer
openingQuestion: NPV = −1 billion (initial investment) + PV(future cash flows) = +200 million. Should this project go ahead?
openingOptions: Yes - a positive NPV means the project creates 200 million of value after discounting
explanation: NPV equals the total present value of future cash flows minus the initial capital outlay. The key word is 'present': cash flows are discounted at the cost of capital, so a positive NPV means the project earns more than the minimum investors require for that level of risk. An NPV of zero isn't a failure - it means the project pays exactly the cost of capital, no more, no less. A negative NPV means the project is destroying value, even if the accounts still show a profit.

diagram.label: Forecast free cash flow year by year
Discount back to today at the cost of capital
Positive means it beats the cost of capital; zero is breakeven at exactly the required rate

realWorldExample.company: A manufacturing group's decision to open a new plant
realWorldExample.description: Before deciding to invest trillions of VND in a new plant, large corporations always build a detailed NPV model - forecasting cash flows over several years, discounted at WACC - to answer the core question: does this project actually create value for shareholders?

quiz.question: What makes NPV most sensitive?
options: The discount rate and the cash flow forecast - small errors give very different results
The number of years, because a longer project always gives a proportionally larger NPV
The initial investment cost, because that's the only truly certain number
The tax rate, because tax determines most of the eventual cash flow
quiz.explanation: NPV is sensitive to: (1) the discount rate - a 2% increase can flip NPV from positive to negative; (2) the FCF forecast - optimistic bias is common in corporate finance. Sensitivity analysis is essential.

quiz.question: A project has an NPV of exactly 0 (neither positive nor negative). What does this mean economically?
options: NPV = 0 means the project will lose exactly the amount of the initial investment
The project earns exactly the cost of capital - it breaks even economically
The project is not worth doing at all because it creates no profit
NPV = 0 can't happen in reality because there's always some margin of error
quiz.explanation: NPV = 0 is the equilibrium point: the project earns exactly what an investor could earn elsewhere at the same level of risk - not bad, but no particular reason to prioritize it either.

quiz.question: Investment of 500 billion, PV of all future cash flows is 560 billion. What is the NPV and what should be done?
options: −60 billion, don't do it because the cost exceeds the benefit
+1.12 times, do it because the ratio is greater than 1
+60 billion, do it because the project genuinely creates additional value
+560 billion, do it because all the cash flows are positive
quiz.explanation: NPV = 560 − 500 = +60 billion. This number can be read directly: the project increases the firm's value by 60 billion in today's money, after fully covering the cost of capital.

quiz.question: Why does raising the discount rate reduce NPV?
options: Because the tax payable rises as the cost of capital rises
Because the initial investment gets multiplied by the interest rate
Because the cash flows of the early years are excluded from the calculation
Because every future cash flow gets discounted more heavily
quiz.explanation: The initial investment sits at time 0 so it isn't discounted at all; only the future cash flow shrinks. That's why a marginal project can flip from worthwhile to not worthwhile just because rates rise 2%.

quiz.question: Two projects have the same NPV of +100 billion, but project A needs 200 billion of capital while B needs 2,000 billion. How should you choose?
options: A, because it creates the same value on a base of capital ten times smaller
B, because a larger scale means a larger impact
They're equal, because the NPV criterion gives an identical result
It can't be decided without knowing the payback period
quiz.explanation: NPV says nothing about the return per unit of capital deployed. When capital is scarce - and it always is - you need a profitability index (NPV/investment) to rank them, or you'll pour all your capital into one bloated project.

keyTakeaways: NPV > 0: creates value; NPV < 0: destroys value
Sensitive to the discount rate and the FCF forecast
NPV > 0 is the main criterion for accepting a project

practicePrompt.question: An investment project requires 500 million VND today, and after discounting all future cash flows back to the present, the present value of the incoming cash flows is 620 million VND. What is the project's NPV, and should the company invest?
options: NPV = 620 - 500 = 120 million VND (positive) - the project creates value beyond the cost of capital invested, so investing is reasonable
NPV = 620 + 500 = 1,120 million VND, adding the cost and benefit together
NPV always equals 0 if the project is calculated correctly using the discounted cash flow method
No conclusion about NPV can be drawn without knowing the project's exact payback period
practicePrompt.explanation: NPV > 0: creates value; NPV < 0: destroys value. Here NPV = 620 - 500 = 120 million VND (positive), meaning the present value of the incoming cash flow exceeds the initial investment cost - this project is worth undertaking because it creates added value for the company.

summary.keyIdea: NPV > 0: creates value; NPV < 0: destroys value
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Sensitive to the discount rate and the FCF forecast

application.title: Calculate NPV yourself
application.message: Think of a major investment or expense you're considering, estimate the cash flows over the next few years, discount them to today, and subtract the initial cost to get NPV.
application.secondary: If the NPV is negative, that investment may not be worth it no matter how appealing it sounds.

sections.text: NPV (Net Present Value) directly answers the most important question in corporate finance: does an investment project truly create value, once you account for the cost of the capital deployed and the time spent waiting to get that cash flow back?

NPV = Total PV of future cash flows − Initial investment cost. If NPV > 0: the project earns more than its cost of capital - it creates value. NPV < 0: the project earns less than its cost of capital - it destroys value even though it may still show an accounting profit. NPV = 0: the project breaks even exactly at the cost of capital, neither adding nor destroying value.

NPV depends on the two most error-prone inputs in finance: the discount rate and the forecast of future cash flows. Raising the discount rate by just 2% can be enough to flip a project from a positive NPV to a negative one. Likewise, an overly optimistic cash flow forecast - a very common mistake in internal investment proposals - can make a seemingly attractive project actually destroy value. This is why sensitivity analysis is always a required step before approval.

sections.title: Discount each year, then add them up

variables.name: Free cash flow in year t
variables.description: The ACTUAL cash in and out, not accounting profit. Depreciation isn't a cash flow; an increase in working capital is.

variables.name: Cost of capital
variables.description: The minimum return investors demand for the project's level of risk. Usually the firm's WACC, but a riskier-than-average project needs a higher r.

variables.name: Initial outlay
variables.description: Excludes sunk costs - money already spent doesn't depend on whether you go ahead with the project or not.

example.title: A three-year project
example.explanation: Total cash received is 600 on a 500 outlay, which sounds like a 100 profit. But after discounting, the project falls 2.6 short of the required 10% minimum - that's the gap between accounting profit and economic value.

sections.text: Why 200 received in year three is only worth 150 today

Dividing by (1 + r)^t isn't an arbitrary mathematical step. If the cost of capital is 10%, then 150.3 today, invested at that same level of risk, becomes 200 in three years - the two amounts are the SAME, just at different points in time. Discounting is how you bring everything to a common point so they can be added together. The further out a cash flow is, the larger the denominator, so a project's tenth-year cash flow is always worth far less than the number written on the spreadsheet - which is why projects promising most of their value at the very end deserve more suspicion than they look.

sections.label: Move r from 10% to 12%, every project gets worse - but not equally
sections.text: With the same 200/year cash flow above, r = 12% gives PV = 480.4 and NPV = −19.6. Just two percentage points erased 17 units of value. The longer the project, the harder this hit lands, because the exponent t grows larger. So when comparing two projects with different lifespans, don't just compare NPV at a single r - check how their NPVs move across a reasonable range of r.

left.label: NPV speaks in MONEY
left.text: Project A: NPV = 120 million on 500 million of capital. Project B: NPV = 300 million on 5 billion of capital. NPV picks B, because shareholders get 300 million richer, not 120 million.

right.label: IRR speaks in PERCENT
right.text: Same two projects, but A's IRR might be 24% and B's only 14%. IRR picks A. But percentages can't be spent - 24% of a small amount is still less money than 14% of a large one.

items: NPV > 0 is the core criterion for accepting an investment project
Between mutually exclusive projects, choose the one with the highest NPV (not the highest IRR)
NPV measures absolute value (in money), unlike IRR which measures a percentage return
Always check NPV's sensitivity to the discount rate before making a final decision

lines: A positive NPV means: the project earns more than investors demand for its level of risk - that is the definition of creating value.
The next lesson moves to IRR: the same cash flow, but asking the reverse question - what percentage return does this project earn?
